teaser: Two fishermen, no faces, and a net full of silver: the picture that taught America what the sea costs.
review_notes:
Opening claim that this type of image shaped the popular figure of the fisherman in oilskins is an interpretation; Bellows and Rockwell Kent painting the Maine coast (Monhegan) in Homer's wake is well documented.
Homer at Cullercoats, England, 1881 to 1882; settled at Prouts Neck, Maine, in 1883.
1884 herring run off Prouts Neck; Homer had himself rowed out to the fleet to sketch (the rower is traditionally named as a local boy, Roswell Googins; name left out).
Anecdote of the sign warning of snakes and mice near his studio: widely repeated, check.
Dimensions about 76.5 x 123 cm (30 x 48 in).
The Fog Warning and Lost on the Grand Banks both dated 1885.
The Art Institute received the painting with the Ryerson collection (not stated in lesson).

lesson.text: Picture a fisherman. Chances are he wears a stiff oilskin coat and a wide rain hat, his face is half hidden, and his boat looks far too small for the water around it. Films, book covers and cans of fish have repeated that figure for a century. One of the places American eyes learned it is this canvas.

Painters felt the pull first. In the early 1900s George Bellows and Rockwell Kent traveled to the Maine coast to paint rock, surf and working men in the blunt, unsentimental way Winslow Homer had shown them. What they were chasing started here, in 1885, with two men and a net.

The scene is simple to describe. Two fishermen in a dory, a small flat-bottomed rowing boat, pull a net heavy with herring out of a gray sea. One hauls. The other leans his weight the opposite way. Homer gives you no shore, no sun and no story beyond the job. So where does the force of the picture come from?

lesson.title: The work
lesson.text: Follow the job from the man's hat down to the fish.

spots.title: No face
spots.text: His sou'wester, a waterproof hat with a long brim at the back, shadows his features completely. He is not a portrait of anyone. He stands for every man who did this.

spots.title: The grip
spots.text: His hands close on the wet mesh. The whole pose folds over this point: back bent, shoulders rounded, all his strength going into the net.

spots.title: The counterweight
spots.text: The second figure, smaller, sits on the far edge and leans out over the water. If he did not, the weight of the net would tip the boat.

spots.title: The herring
spots.text: The fish are the only bright things in the picture: quick strokes of white, blue and a touch of red at the gills, caught in a mesh drawn with thin dark lines.

lesson.text: Notice what you did not see: an eye, a mouth, an expression. Homer leaves the men anonymous on purpose. It makes the painting less about two individuals and more about a kind of labor, repeated every day by thousands of people whose names nobody wrote down.

Homer learned to look at fishing people in England. In 1881 and 1882 he lived in Cullercoats, a village on the North Sea, and painted the women who waited on shore and hauled the catch. He came home a more serious painter.

In 1883 he moved for good to Prouts Neck, a rocky point on the coast of Maine, and worked in a converted stable a few steps from the surf. The next year an enormous school of herring arrived offshore and a fleet gathered to take it. Homer had himself rowed out among the boats at dusk and drew what he saw.
He guarded his solitude at Prouts Neck. The story goes that he put up a sign warning passersby of snakes and mice, simply to keep curious visitors away from his studio.

Back on land he rebuilt those sketches into something much more solid than a snapshot. The canvas is about 76 by 123 centimeters, 30 by 48 inches, and the men fill it like a monument. The trick is geometry.
Two shapes organize the whole picture.

lines.label: A pyramid
lines.text: Men and boat lock into one triangle with the hauler's hat at the top. A pyramid is the steadiest shape there is, which is why these two feel so firmly planted.

lines.label: The swell
lines.text: Under them, nothing is steady. A dark wave lifts the middle of the boat and drops away on both sides. Stability sits on top of pure motion.

lines.label: Oars and net
lines.text: The oars lean one way and the net slides off the other, making a second, looser angle that spills the catch toward the right edge.

lesson.text: Homer makes ordinary work look heroic without a single heroic gesture. He hides the faces, builds the bodies into a pyramid, and lets the sea do the threatening.

And the sea does threaten. Dories like this one did not go out alone. They were lowered from a larger sailing ship, a schooner, fished for hours, then rowed back to be hoisted aboard. Everything depended on finding that ship again. Now look at the weather Homer chose.
The men's way home is somewhere in this fog. Can you find a ship?

spots.title: Ghost sails
spots.text: Pale sails stand on the horizon, almost the same color as the sky. There is another on the far left. A little more fog and they vanish, and the dory is on its own.

lesson.text: The same year, 1885, Homer painted two companion scenes that say this out loud. In The Fog Warning a lone man in a dory looks over his shoulder at a schooner slipping away. Lost on the Grand Banks shows two men peering over the side into mist. Here, the danger stays a whisper at the edge.

The palette is nearly colorless. Sky, coats, boat and water are mixed from grays and browns, so that the small flashes of silver, blue and red on the fish, and the orange float bobbing at the bottom, hit your eye like sparks.

After this picture Homer's people slowly shrank and the ocean took over his canvases, until in his last years he often painted waves and rock with no one there at all. Standing in front of these two bent backs, you might ask what he had already decided: is this a painting about men, or about the thing they are up against?

quiz.question: Why can't you see the fishermen's faces?
options: The paint has darkened with age
Their rain hats put them in shadow, keeping them anonymous
They are turned away from the catch
quiz.explanation: Homer hides them under sou'westers so they stand for a whole kind of labor.

quiz.question: What is a dory?
quiz.explanation: Dories were lowered from schooners and rowed out to fish.

quiz.question: What does the smaller figure on the left do?
options: He leans out to balance the weight of the net
quiz.explanation: Without his counterweight, the heavy net would tip the boat.

quiz.question: Where did Homer see the herring fleet that inspired the painting?
quiz.explanation: A huge school of herring arrived off Prouts Neck in 1884 and he was rowed out to sketch.

quiz.question: What quiet sign of danger sits on the horizon?
quiz.explanation: If the fog hides the mother ship, the dory cannot find its way back.

facts.text: Homer painted this scene on a sunny afternoon with the coast in view.
facts.explanation: There is no shore and no sun, only gray fog and open water.

facts.text: The two men and their boat are arranged in a pyramid shape.
facts.explanation: The hauler's hat forms the top of a steady triangle set on a moving swell.

facts.text: Homer never left the United States before painting The Herring Net.
facts.explanation: He had lived in the English fishing village of Cullercoats in 1881 and 1882.
